passages.text: The Asch conformity experiment has recently gained considerable attention as a way of measuring conformity in large language models (LLMs). While previous studies have focused on demonstrating conformity in LLMs, our work adds a further quantitative layer to this approach. Instead of sampling a frontier LLM on a suite of questions, our approach samples a single question repeatedly, leveraging the probabilistic nature of LLMs to produce a distribution of answers. In doing so, we can compare the distributions of answers before and after the model is presented with the manufactured consensus. Our experiments confirm that frontier LLMs do conform, reinforcing prior literature, and, through our distribution-to-distribution comparisons, provide additional quantitative data on the conditions that lead to conformity and the degree to which it occurs.

The Asch conformity experiment Asch (1956) is a prime example of the second approach, and it has been repeated with LLM subjects (see e.g. Bito et al. (2026); Zhu et al. (2024); Bajaj and Tiganj (2026); Weng et al. (2025); Choi et al. (2025); Baltaji et al. (2024)) to study how LLMs conform to a perceived consensus. This is an increasingly important topic given the rise of agentic systems, in which LLM agents interact with one another and possibly with human beings. These studies compare the answers of an LLM to multiple-choice questions on its own and after being told of a manufactured consensus answer, and they measure conformity as how often the LLM adopts the consensus answer across many different questions.

We now describe our methodology for measuring conformity in LLMs. We keep the elements of the Asch experiment and replace the line judgment with a task that is natural for an LLM, that is, choosing the word that fills the blank of a sentence (Figure 1). Specifically, the line that matches the standard becomes the word the model writes most often, and the comparison lines become candidate words. Just as Asch varied how much a wrong line differed from the standard, we vary how a candidate word differs from the model’s most frequent word, either in how strongly the model prefers it or in how close its meaning is. The confederates become other participants whose answers appear in the prompt.

Unlike a human subject, an LLM can answer the same question many times under identical conditions, so we sample the model in repeated independent trials and compare its answer distribution when alone with its answer distribution after it sees the answers of the other participants.

One of the main reasons, however, that the Asch conformity experiment was so successful was that its task (see Figure 1) was easy and natural for humans. The subject judged which of three comparison lines matched a standard line after several confederates had given their answers, and on most trials the confederates unanimously gave the same wrong answer. Wrong answers that matched this consensus could thus readily be attributed to social pressure, for which there is no meaningful analog in the LLM setting.

The purpose of this paper is to perform a conformity experiment that leverages the unique properties of LLMs. First, we need a task that is “easy and natural” for an LLM, and we chose 2015-era SAT-style fill-in-the-blank sentences, as providing a missing word in context is closely related to the word prediction that LLMs are trained on. Second, rather than utilizing social pressure, we leverage the inherently probabilistic nature of LLMs.

Our results confirm that all six frontier LLMs we test conform, which reinforces previous studies in the literature. More than that, however, they show that the degree of conformity depends on the consensus answer. The models conform most toward another of their preferred-model-words, but they also conform considerably toward words they did not output on their own when these words are close in meaning to their preferred word, and they almost never conform toward words far in meaning. On average, conformity also grows with the number of reported other participants up to five and changes little between five and ten.

output.title: A Quantitative Approach to Asch Conformity in Frontier Large Language Models

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as an effective post-training paradigm for enhancing the video reasoning capability of Large Multimodal Models (LMMs). papers.abstract: A full-duplex spoken dialogue model must yield when the user cuts in and hold when the user merely backchannels. A binary window reward gives zero advantage on exactly the windows that most need learning (a zero-gradient trap), and the one score per rollout is spread over listening-state decisions the reward is not written in terms of (credit leakage), so the model talks into silence or stops answering. Both come from sampling a reward that is a known function of a few binary control decisions. We propose \emph{window likelihood} (\WL): sample a continuation per window, but integrate in closed form over the stop decisions it visits and maximise the log-probability of acting correctly---a noisy-OR for yielding, a survival product for holding. On HumDial-FDBench, \WL\ gives the best yield/hold F1 on all six structurally different open models we post-train, exceeds Kyutai's released GRPO checkpoints (trained on different data), and adds no re-opening of the floor on any model.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly trained to abstain from answering questions they are unsure about. However, this ability is often misapplied: in real-world applications, user prompts sometimes contain elements of uncertainty, which lead LLMs to abstain even on problems they are capable of solving. passages.text: With the two abstention paradigms placed on common ground, we ask whether abstention training outperforms selective answering, and if so, where this advantage comes from.

Abstention mitigates hallucination by withholding answers that are likely to be wrong. Formally, consider a dataset \mathcal{D}=\{(x_{i},y_{i}^{*})\}_{i=1}^{N} of N questions, where x_{i} is a question and y_{i}^{*} is its reference answer. An abstention method takes a question x_{i} and either returns an answer \hat{y}_{i} or abstains, partitioning the dataset into an answered set \mathcal{A} and an abstained set \mathcal{R} . Ideally, all correct answers should remain in \mathcal{A} and all others should fall into \mathcal{R} . Real methods fall short in both directions, causing a trade-off between the fraction of questions answered and the error rate among those answers.

Metrics commonly adopted by prior abstention training studies fail to fully characterize this trade-off. Abstention is neither correct nor incorrect, but any single score over all questions must assign it a value relative to the other two. Prior studies do so implicitly (Yang et al., 2024; Cheng et al., 2024): overall accuracy values an abstention as an incorrect answer, hallucination rate values it as a correct answer, and composites such as accuracy minus hallucination rate (Wei et al., 2026) value it midway between the two. Under any such valuation, a difference in score need not reflect better abstention decisions. It may simply reflect a different amount of abstention: withholding answers at random, for instance, lowers the hallucination rate without improving a single decision. Accuracy over the answered questions alone (Zhang et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2026) sidesteps the valuation by ignoring abstentions, but then omits the coverage they cost. These metrics thus suffice to describe one policy at its native coverage, but cannot fairly compare policies with different coverages.

papers.abstract: We introduce Heads of Security (HoS), a prompt injection defense that enforces instruction-data separation via a small set of learned per-head attention gates. HoS learns how each head should redistribute attention between trusted and untrusted tokens, enabling models to reason over untrusted content without following injected instructions. We evaluate HoS on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and GPT-OSS-20B. We compare it against SecAlign++, a state-of-the-art finetuning-based defense, and ASIDE, a defense that, like ours, builds instruction-data separation into the model architecture. We show that HoS offers greater robustness to adaptive attacks, better performance on standard utility benchmarks, and matches top performance on standard agentic prompt injection benchmarks. More specifically, the black-box RL-Hammer attack reaches 97% ASR against GPT-OSS-20B and 85% against SecAlign, but only 10% against HoS. Claudini, a state-of-the-art white-box attack, strengthened against HoS through autoresearch, requires 3 times more FLOPs to reach the same ASR on HoS as it does on GPT-OSS-20B or SecAlign. HoS preserves base-model utility across standard multiple-choice benchmarks and prompting setups, whereas SecAlign and ASIDE degrade in few-shot settings. On agentic benchmarks with static attacks, HoS and SecAlign perform similarly and substantially improve the security-utility trade-off over the base model. ASIDE struggles with tool use, achieving only 10% utility. These results show that prompt injection robustness can be achieved and improved through targeted attention interventions.
